claim: RecQ helicases promote genomic stability through their unique ability to suppress illegitimate recombination and resolve recombination intermediates.
source: RecQ helicases promote genomic stability through their unique ability to suppress illegitimate recombination and resolve recombination intermediates.
evidence: This is a general statement about RecQ helicase function that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: DNA structure-specific activities of RecQ helicases are mediated by the helicase-and-RNAseD like C-terminal (HRDC) domain.
source: These DNA structure-specific activities of RecQ helicases are mediated by the helicase-and-RNAseD like C-terminal (HRDC) domain, via unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research knowledge, though the mechanisms are stated as unknown.

claim: The HRDC domain stabilizes intrinsic, sequence-dependent pauses of the core helicase in a DNA geometry-dependent manner.
source: Here, employing single-molecule magnetic tweezers and rapid kinetic approaches we establish that the HRDC domain stabilizes intrinsic, sequence-dependent, pauses of the core helicase (lacking the HRDC) in a DNA geometry-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from single-molecule magnetic tweezers and rapid kinetic approaches.

claim: The unwinding rate of RecQ depends on the stability of the duplex DNA leading to transient sequence-dependent pauses.
source: We elucidate the core unwinding mechanism in which the unwinding rate depends on the stability of the duplex DNA leading to transient sequence-dependent pauses.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The HRDC domain causes non-linear amplification of transient pauses through controlled binding.
source: We further demonstrate a non-linear amplification of these transient pauses by the controlled binding of the HRDC domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experimental data and kinetic modeling.

claim: DNA sequence- and geometry-dependent pausing may underlie a homology sensing mechanism that allows rapid disruption of unstable (illegitimate) and stabilization of stable (legitimate) DNA strand invasions.
source: The resulting DNA sequence- and geometry-dependent pausing may underlie a homology sensing mechanism that allows rapid disruption of unstable (illegitimate) and stabilization of stable (legitimate) DNA strand invasions, which suggests an intrinsic mechanism of recombination quality control by RecQ helicases.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings regarding the biological function of the observed mechanism.

claim: Escherichia coli RecQ helicase is the founding member of the RecQ family.
source: Escherichia coli RecQ (Ec RecQ) helicase is the founding member of the family (Nakayama et al., 1984) and plays roles in both suppressing illegitimate recombination and facilitating various steps of DNA recombinational repair (Hanada et al., 1997; Ryder et al., 1994; León-Ortiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nakayama et al., 1984.

claim: E. coli RecQ plays roles in both suppressing illegitimate recombination and facilitating various steps of DNA recombinational repair.
source: Escherichia coli RecQ (Ec RecQ) helicase is the founding member of the family (Nakayama et al., 1984) and plays roles in both suppressing illegitimate recombination and facilitating various steps of DNA recombinational repair (Hanada et al., 1997; Ryder et al., 1994; León-Ortiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hanada et al., 1997; Ryder et al., 1994; León-Ortiz et al., 2018.

claim: RecQ helicases are highly conserved from bacteria to humans.
source: RecQ helicases are highly conserved from bacteria to humans and eukaryotic RecQ helicases have been shown to play similar pro- and anti-recombination functions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RecQ helicase conservation.

claim: Most unicellular organisms express a single RecQ homolog, whereas multi-cellular organisms often possess multiple RecQ helicases specialized to different roles.
source: Most unicellular organisms, such as E. coli and yeast, express a single RecQ homolog, whereas multi-cellular organisms often possess multiple RecQ helicases specialized to different roles in genome maintenance processes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RecQ helicase distribution across organisms.

claim: The fundamental conserved activity of RecQ helicases is the ATP-dependent unwinding of double-stranded DNA.
source: The fundamental conserved activity of RecQ helicases is the ATP-dependent unwinding of double-stranded DNA (Nakayama et al., 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nakayama et al., 1984.

claim: All RecQ members possess two evolutionarily conserved RecA-like helicase domains with an ATP binding and hydrolysis site located in a cleft between them.
source: All RecQ members possess two evolutionarily conserved RecA-like helicase domains with an ATP binding and hydrolysis site located in a cleft between them (Bennett and Keck, 2004; Chu and Hickson, 2009; Bachrati and Hickson, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bennett and Keck, 2004; Chu and Hickson, 2009; Bachrati and Hickson, 2008.

claim: The RecQ C-terminal domain (RQC) comprises zinc binding and winged-helix (WH) sub-domains associated with protein structural integrity and duplex DNA binding, respectively.
source: The RecQ C-terminal domain (RQC) comprises zinc binding and winged-helix (WH) sub-domains associated with protein structural integrity and duplex DNA binding, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RecQ domain structure and function.

claim: Many RecQ-family members possess an accessory single-stranded DNA-binding module termed the helicase-and-RNAseD-C-terminal (HRDC) domain.
source: Although less conserved, many RecQ-family members, including Ec RecQ and multiple human RecQ homologs, possess an accessory single-stranded (ss) DNA-binding module termed the helicase-and-RNAseD-C-terminal (HRDC) domain (Bernstein and Keck, 2005; Vindigni and Hickson, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bernstein and Keck, 2005; Vindigni and Hickson, 2009.

claim: The HRDC domain is generally dispensable for helicase activity but is critical for certain recombination intermediate processing steps.
source: The HRDC, while generally dispensable for helicase activity, is critical for certain recombination intermediate processing steps, such as disruption of displacement strand (D-loop) invasion and double Holliday junction resolution (Rezazadeh, 2012; Singh et al., 2012; Chatterjee et al., 2014; Harami et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rezazadeh, 2012; Singh et al., 2012; Chatterjee et al., 2014; Harami et al., 2017.

claim: Full length RecQ has a higher ssDNA binding affinity than RecQ constructs lacking the HRDC.
source: Biochemical studies have established that full length RecQ has a higher ssDNA binding affinity than RecQ constructs lacking the HRDC, which is consistent with the findings that the interaction between the HRDC and ssDNA contributes to DNA substrate specificity of RecQ helicases (Bernstein and Keck, 2005; Vindigni and Hickson, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bernstein and Keck, 2005; Vindigni and Hickson, 2009.

claim: HRDC interactions contribute to DNA substrate-geometry dependent binding orientation and unwinding by RecQ.
source: Recently, we provided evidence that HRDC interactions contribute to DNA substrate-geometry dependent binding orientation and unwinding by RecQ, and demonstrated that these HRDC-mediated interactions play a role in suppressing illegitimate recombination in E. coli (Harami et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Harami et al., 2017, which is prior work by the authors.

claim: The HRDC strongly favors binding of RecQ to D-loop structures in an orientation that promotes disruption of the invading DNA strand.
source: Whereas these findings indicate that the HRDC strongly favors binding of RecQ to D-loop structures in an orientation that promotes disruption of the invading DNA strand (Harami et al., 2017), it is not clear how RecQ can subsequently discriminate between homologous and non-homologous strand invasions; once correctly oriented on the D-loop, RecQ can unwind any invading strand and indiscriminately disrupt all D-loop formations.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Harami et al., 2017.

claim: HRDC-dependent pausing during hairpin DNA unwinding occurs repeatedly at distinct positions on the DNA hairpin.
source: In this work we identify a potential solution to this quandary, suggested by the observation that HRDC-dependent pausing during hairpin DNA unwinding is not random but occurs repeatedly at distinct positions on the DNA hairpin.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: RecQWT and RecQ-dH show different pausing behavior during DNA hairpin unwinding, with RecQWT showing frequent pausing and strand-switching.
source: As described previously (Harami et al., 2017), frequent pausing and strand-switching by WT RecQ (RecQWT) is caused by the HRDC as the HRDC deletion mutant (RecQ-dH) shows significantly less pausing during DNA hairpin unwinding (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1B and a citation to Harami et al., 2017.

claim: Pausing is attributed to transient binding of the HRDC domain to the displaced single-stranded DNA behind RecQ.
source: Pausing is attributed to transient binding of the HRDC domain to the displaced single-stranded DNA behind RecQ.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental observations and prior work.

claim: HRDC binding to duplex DNA ahead of the helicase or to the translocation strand of ssDNA behind the helicase are ruled out by the lack of pauses during unwinding of a 'gapped' DNA substrate.
source: HRDC binding to either duplex DNA ahead of the helicase, or to the translocation strand of ssDNA behind the helicase, are ruled out by the lack of pauses during the unwinding of a 'gapped' DNA substrate in which the displaced strand is not constrained (Harami et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Harami et al., 2017.

claim: The dwell-time histogram for RecQWT unwinding traces exhibits peaks at distinct positions along the hairpin.
source: Interestingly, the dwell-time histogram as a function of position for RecQWT unwinding traces exhibits peaks at distinct positions along the hairpin (Figure 2A; top).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The peak locations of pausing and duplex stability are highly correlated for RecQWT.
source: We found that the peak locations of pausing and duplex stability were highly correlated (Figure 2A; bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pause positions from the dwell time histogram of RecQWT are linearly correlated with peak positions from the DNA base-pair energy profile with a slope of 0.99 ± 0.03, Pearson's r of 0.97, and χ2 = 0.85.
source: Consistent with this observation, pause positions from the dwell time histogram of RecQWT were linearly correlated with peak positions from the DNA base-pair energy profile (Figure 2B; top) with a slope of 0.99 ± 0.03, linear correlation coefficient (Pearson's r) of 0.97, and χ2 = 0.85, indicating a strong linear correlation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The sequence around the peak positions contains a high percentage of GC (~70%).
source: The sequence around the peak positions (±4 bp) contained a high percentage of GC (~70%), consistent with the finding that the pause positions are related to the duplex stability of the DNA.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis of the DNA substrate.

claim: The pause positions of RecQ-dH are linearly correlated with the duplex stability peaks, returning a slope of 0.96 ± 0.06, Pearson's r = 0.95, and χ2 = 1.1.
source: The pause positions for RecQ-dH were obtained from dwell time histograms following the same procedure used for RecQWT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and plotted as a function of the peak positions of DNA base-pair stability (Figure 2B). The pause positions of RecQ-dH were linearly correlated with the duplex stability peaks, returning a slope of 0.96 ± 0.06, Pearson's r = 0.95, and χ2 = 1.1.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The pause positions of RecQ-dH are statistically identical to those of RecQWT.
source: Moreover, the pause positions of RecQ-dH are statistically identical to those of RecQWT, confirming that HRDC-dependent pausing likely originates from stabilization of sequence-dependent unwinding kinetics of RecQ helicase.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of the experimental data.

claim: The roughly 20-fold difference in the time the enzyme requires to unwind DNA at the longest pause duration sites in comparison to the average unwinding rate suggests that more than a single base pair is being opened by the enzyme during each kinetic step.
source: However, the roughly 20-fold difference in the time the enzyme requires to unwind DNA at the longest pause duration sites in comparison to the average unwinding rate, suggests that more than a single base pair is being opened by the enzyme during each kinetic step.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and theoretical considerations.

claim: Pausing is governed by a combination of the DNA base-pair stability and the number of base pairs melted by the helicase during each kinetic step.
source: Following this simple analysis, we suggest that pausing is governed by a combination of the DNA base-pair stability and the number of base pairs melted by the helicase during each kinetic step.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: During processive unwinding, the melting step is the rate limiting step that determines the unwinding rate and pause durations.
source: During processive unwinding, this melting step is the rate limiting step that determines the unwinding rate and pause durations.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism based on the experimental observations.

claim: The delayed release model with a 5 bp kinetic step better describes RecQ-dH unwinding than the simultaneous melting model.
source: For the delayed release model, χν2 reached a minimum around 5 bp (χν2 = 0.9x10−1), lower than the minimum for simultaneous melting model that reached a minimum at 2 bp (χν2 = 1.4x10−1). This suggests that a delayed release scenario may describe the unwinding mechanism of core RecQ.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling and comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The unwinding rate of RecQ-dH decreases with increasing Na+ concentration.
source: We varied the Na+ concentration from 25 to 500 mM while maintaining Mg2+ at 5 mM under otherwise identical buffer conditions. The unwinding rate of RecQ-dH decreased with increasing Na+ concentration.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from varying Na+ concentration.

claim: The relative decrease in unwinding rate with Na+ concentration is better described by the delayed release model with a 5 bp kinetic step than the simultaneous 2 bp DNA melting model.
source: The relative decrease in unwinding rate was much better described by the delayed release model with a 5 bp kinetic step. than the simultaneous 2 bp DNA melting model (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of experimental data with computational models shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Unwinding traces comprised a short (~0.1 s) initial lag, followed by a biphasic appearance of the labeled ssDNA reaction product.
source: Unwinding traces comprised a short (~0.1 s) initial lag, followed by a biphasic appearance of the labeled ssDNA reaction product (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the ensemble kinetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Global fitting of the unwinding kinetics revealed smallest χv2 values for an apparent kinetic step size of 5 bp for both RecQ and RecQ-dH.
source: Using a modified version of the n-step model (Figure 4C), global fitting of the unwinding kinetics of the gc36, gc48 and gc79 substrates using an integer series of n ranging from 1 to 7 revealed smallest χv2 values for an apparent kinetic step size of 5 bp for both RecQ and RecQ-dH (Figure 4B–D) with all DNA substrates, similar to that suggested by our MT results (Figure 3A–B) and by previous findings (Lin et al., 2017; Harami et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from kinetic modeling of ensemble experimental data shown in Figure 4, supported by citations to Lin et al., 2017; Harami et al., 2015.

claim: The smallest χv2 value was obtained for the delayed release model with a kinetic step size of 4 bp for RecQ-dH and 5 bp for RecQWT.
source: In agreement with the results of the MT analysis (Figure 3C), the smallest χv2 value was obtained for the delayed release model with a kinetic step size of 4 bp for RecQ-dH and 5 bp for RecQWT (Figure 4B and C, other parameters are listed in Supplementary file 1 Table S2).
evidence: This is a finding from kinetic modeling of ensemble experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Decreasing the ATP concentration resulted in frequent and extensive enzyme backsliding.
source: We found that decreasing the ATP concentration (sufficiently lowering the unwinding rate) resulted in frequent and extensive enzyme backsliding (observable as rapid partial rezipping of the hairpin during an unwinding event), which complicates kinetic step size measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experiments at low ATP concentration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATPγS showed a comparable binding affinity to ATP with a significantly shorter binding time (~1 s) than AMP-PNP.
source: On the other hand, ATPγS, showed a comparable binding affinity to ATP with a significantly shorter binding time (~1 s) than AMP-PNP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments comparing ATP analogs shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The unwinding rate decreased with increasing ATPγS fraction.
source: We measured the unwinding activity of RecQ-dH at different fractions of ATPγS (0.05–0.5 mM) while keeping the total combined concentration of ATP and ATPγS constant at 1 mM. The unwinding rate decreased with increasing ATPγS fraction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The estimated step size of RecQ-dH converged from ~8 bp at a low ATPγS fraction to 5 bp at higher ATPγS fractions.
source: We found that the estimated step size of RecQ-dH from both step-finding algorithms were comparable, converging from ~8 bp at a low ATPγS fraction to 5 bp at higher ATPγS fractions, suggesting that the average kinetic step size of RecQ-dH is 5 bp [T-test: 5.3 ± 0.1 (center); 3.0 ± 0.6 (Standard Deviation); Kerssemakers: 5.2 ± 0.1(center); 2.1 ± 0.1 (Standard Deviation), errors correspond to the standard deviations from Gaussian fitting].
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from step-size analysis shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The average kinetic step size of RecQ-dH is 5 bp.
source: We found that the estimated step size of RecQ-dH from both step-finding algorithms were comparable, converging from ~8 bp at a low ATPγS fraction to 5 bp at higher ATPγS fractions, suggesting that the average kinetic step size of RecQ-dH is 5 bp [T-test: 5.3 ± 0.1 (center); 3.0 ± 0.6 (Standard Deviation); Kerssemakers: 5.2 ± 0.1(center); 2.1 ± 0.1 (Standard Deviation), errors correspond to the standard deviations from Gaussian fitting].
evidence: This is a conclusion from the step-size analysis with quantitative support.

claim: A 2.5 bp kinetic step was occasionally observed at 500 µM ATPγS.
source: In line with this, we occasionally observed a 2.5 bp kinetic step at 500 µM ATPγS, and the step-size distribution at lower ATPγS fractions included peaks at 7.5, 10, and 12.5 bp, consistent with a fundamental step-size of 2.5 bp corresponding to the release of one ssDNA strand of 5 nt (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: RecQ exhibits tight mechano-chemical coupling with C = 1.0 ± 0.2 bp/ATP.
source: From this global fitting, we found that C = 1.0 ± 0.2 bp/ATP, kATP/ kATPγS = 1.2 ± 0.2, and 1/koffATPγS = 0.4 ± 0.1 s suggesting a tight mechano-chemical coupling in agreement with previous ensemble measurements (Harami et al., 2015; Sarlós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from global fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 5D, supported by citations to Harami et al., 2015; Sarlós et al., 2012.

claim: RecQWT exhibits occasional repetitive rezipping and unwinding (shuttling) around the pause position.
source: In addition to the sequence dependence, HRDC-dependent pausing exhibits two interesting features: occasional repetitive rezipping and unwinding (shuttling) around the pause position and significantly prolonged pausing durations for certain pausing positions (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HRDC-binding triggers shuttling behavior in which 5–10 bp are repetitively unwound and rezipped at relatively long-lived pause positions.
source: It appears that HRDC-binding triggers this shuttling behavior in which 5–10 bp are repetitively unwound and rezipped at the relatively long-lived (>0.14 s) intrinsic pause positions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The average dwell times for RecQWT are highly non-linearly correlated with the base-pair stability.
source: Indeed, the average dwell times for RecQWT are highly non-linearly correlated with the base-pair stability (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The dwell-times for RecQ-dH scale linearly and much less dramatically with the base-pair stability.
source: In contrast, the dwell-times for RecQ-dH scale linearly and much less dramatically with the base-pair stability (Figure 6A), indicating that the HRDC-stabilized pausing can be described as a non-linear amplifier of the intrinsic sequence-dependent unwinding kinetics.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A simple kinetic competition model cannot reproduce the dramatic changes in pause probability observed for RecQWT hairpin unwinding.
source: We found that a simple kinetic competition model in which HRDC binding is in kinetic competition with the forward motion of the helicase (Appendix 1) cannot reproduce the dramatic changes in pause probability observed for RecQWT hairpin unwinding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from kinetic modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pausing duration distribution for RecQwt is better described by a double rather than single exponential distribution.
source: In line with this, the pausing duration distribution for RecQwt is better described by a double rather than single exponential distribution (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RecQWT has two pause lifetimes of 1.8 ± 0.3 s and 0.4 ± 0.1 s.
source: Both pause lifetimes (1.8 ± 0.3 s and 0.4 ± 0.1 s) are longer than the average pause duration (0.14 ± 0.03 s, see SI) for the core RecQ (RecQ-dH), indicating that there are multiple HRDC-dependent pause states.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of pause duration distributions.

claim: Pausing of RecQWT around the 90 bp unwound hairpin position was significantly reduced when a mismatch was present at 90 bp.
source: We found that pausing of RecQWT around the 90 bp unwound hairpin position was significantly reduced compared to intact 174 bp hairpin when a mismatch was present at 90 bp and additional mismatch at 124 bp further suppressed pausing around 120 bp (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from mismatch experiments shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The prominent peaks in the dwell time histogram of the intact hairpin DNA were diminished one by one with the introduction of mismatches at the corresponding positions.
source: The prominent peaks in the dwell time histogram of the intact hairpin DNA were diminished one by one with the introduction of mismatches at the corresponding positions confirming the correlation between pausing and homology (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from mismatch experiments shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pronounced pausing of WT RecQ at GC rich sequences results from two amplification steps that convert the ~kBT energy differences between GC and AT base pairs to a robust readout of sequence stability.
source: The pronounced pausing of WT RecQ at GC rich sequences results from two amplification steps that convert the ~kBT energy differences between GC and AT base pairs to a robust readout of sequence stability (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The first amplification step arises from the basic mechanochemistry of DNA unwinding that involves a ~ 5 bp kinetic step.
source: The first amplification step arises from the basic mechanochemistry of DNA unwinding that involves a ~ 5 bp kinetic step in which ~ 5 bp of DNA are unwound in 5 rounds of ATP hydrolysis followed by release of the two DNA strands.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The second amplification step involves the non-linear amplification of the intrinsic difference in unwinding rate through the binding and stabilization of short sequence-dependent pauses by the HRDC.
source: The second amplification step involves the non-linear amplification of the intrinsic difference in unwinding rate in proportion to GC content through the binding and stabilization of short sequence-dependent pauses by the HRDC.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The two rounds of linear and non-linear amplification result in strong sequence dependent pausing of WT RecQ that results in a greater than 10-fold difference in average unwinding rate of legitimate versus illegitimate paired sequences.
source: Together these two rounds of linear and non-linear amplification result in strong sequence dependent pausing of WT RecQ on hairpin substrates that results in a greater than 10-fold difference in average unwinding rate of legitimate versus illegitimate paired sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and mechanistic interpretation.

claim: A recent single molecule study of E. coli RecQWT indicated a switching behavior between a fast unwinding mode and a slower unwinding mode.
source: A recent single molecule study of E. coli RecQWT indicated a switching behavior between a fast unwinding mode, similar to that of RecQ-dH, and a slower unwinding mode that is similar but not identical to what we observed for RecQWT unwinding in the present study (Bagchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bagchi et al., 2018.

claim: RecQ hydrolyzes 5 ATP molecules during a 5 bp kinetic unwinding step that concludes with asynchronous release of two five nt ssDNA segments on average.
source: We find that RecQ hydrolyzes 5 ATP molecules during a 5 bp kinetic unwinding step that concludes with asynchronous release of two five nt ssDNA segments on average (Figures 3–5).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings shown in Figures 3–5.

claim: ATP binding likely stimulates RecQ binding to and melting of DNA duplex prior to hydrolysis.
source: Furthermore, ATP binding likely stimulates RecQ binding to and melting of DNA duplex prior to hydrolysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: E. coli RecQ helicase was identified as an active helicase based on the minimal force and DNA sequence dependence of duplex unwinding in previous single molecule experiments.
source: In previous single molecule experiments, E. coli RecQ helicase was identified as an active helicase based on the minimal force and DNA sequence dependence of duplex unwinding (Manosas et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Manosas et al., 2010.

claim: RecQ unwinds one base-pair per ATP hydrolysis cycle.
source: The mechano-chemical coupling is a measure of how many chemical cycles an enzyme completes to take one mechanical step. In the case of RecQ or other helicases, it corresponds to how many ATP molecules are consumed per one base translocation (or base-pair unwound for unwinding). For translocation, RecQ shows a tight coupling close to one nucleotide step per ATP hydrolysis (Sarlós et al., 2012). Our study reveals that the mechano-chemical coupling for unwinding maintains one base-pair melting per ATP hydrolysis (Figure 4C), which is also supported by the results of a recent single-molecule florescence study of RecQ unwinding (Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4C, supported by citations to Sarlós et al., 2012 and Lin et al., 2017.

claim: DNA melting precedes ATP hydrolysis in the proposed kinetic model.
source: The proposed kinetic model based on our ATP dependent kinetic analysis (Appendix 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggests that DNA melting precedes ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from kinetic modeling based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATP binding stabilizes the DNA-RecQ interaction and facilitates DNA melting presumably coupled to an ATP binding-dependent conformational change of RecQ.
source: In this model, ATP binding stabilizes the DNA-RecQ interaction and facilitates DNA melting presumably coupled to an ATP binding-dependent conformational change of RecQ such as rotation of the helicase domains relative to one another, which explains more frequent backsliding under lower ATP concentration (Bernstein et al., 2003; Manthei et al., 2015; Pike et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 2003; Manthei et al., 2015; Pike et al., 2009.

claim: Recent structural results suggest that RecQ binding may melt two base-pairs of DNA before ATP binding.
source: Recent structural results suggest that RecQ binding may melt two base-pairs of DNA before ATP binding (Manthei et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Manthei et al., 2015.

claim: A 'Guanine binding pocket' located in the helicase domain specifically interacts with guanine bases to destabilize G-quadruplex structures.
source: Whereas we establish that pausing arises from the stability of DNA duplex, recent work by Voter et. al suggests an alternative mechanism for sequence-dependent pausing. In their work, they identify a 'Guanine binding pocket' located in the helicase domain that specifically interacts with guanine bases to destabilize G-quadruplex structures.
evidence: This statement refers to work by Voter et al. and is supported by citation.

claim: The HRDC regulates the binding orientation of RecQ core to promote disruption of D-loop structures.
source: It has been shown that the HRDC regulates the binding orientation of RecQ core to promote disruption of D-loop structures, early homologous recombination intermediates (Harami et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Harami et al., 2017.

claim: ssDNA binding by the HRDC is not random but occurs at DNA sequences where the helicase core pauses due to the high duplex stability.
source: Our present study reveals that the HRDC-ssDNA interactions are strongly coupled to DNA sequence-dependent pausing of the RecQ helicase core: ssDNA binding by the HRDC is not random but occurs at DNA sequences where the helicase core pauses due to the high duplex stability (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Either a low homology (base-pair mismatches) or low duplex stability (low GC regions) strongly reduces RecQ pausing.
source: On the other hand, either a low homology (base-pair mismatches) or low duplex stability (low GC regions) strongly reduces RecQ pausing (Figures 2 and 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased illegitimate recombination frequencies are detected in vivo upon compromising RecQ HRDC function.
source: Importantly, this feature can support discrimination between legitimate and illegitimate recombination events by RecQ helicases, in accordance with the increased illegitimate recombination frequencies detected in vivo upon compromising RecQ HRDC function (Harami et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Harami et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016.

claim: The HRDC both targets RecQ to D-loop intermediates and orients the enzyme in a configuration favoring D-loop disruption.
source: Previously we showed that the HRDC both targets RecQ to D-loop intermediates and orients the enzyme in a configuration favoring D-loop disruption (Harami et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Harami et al., 2017.

claim: RecQ-catalyzed unwinding of long and stable D-loops will be frequently interrupted by HRDC-stabilized pauses that drastically decrease the average unwinding rate.
source: RecQ-catalyzed unwinding of long and stable D-loops will be frequently interrupted by HRDC-stabilized pauses that drastically decrease the average unwinding rate.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation and prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: RecQ unwinding of short and/or unstable D-loops will proceed rapidly (60–80 bp/s) resulting in the efficient disruption of the D-loop before it can be further extended.
source: Conversely, RecQ unwinding of short and/or unstable D-loops will proceed rapidly (60–80 bp/s) resulting in the efficient disruption of the D-loop before it can be further extended.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation and prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: The homology sensing mechanism proposed for E. coli RecQ is potentially applicable to the suppression of illegitimate recombination by BLM.
source: Whereas this study focused exclusively on E. coli RecQ, the homology sensing mechanism we propose is potentially applicable to the suppression of illegitimate, or so called 'homeologous recombination' by BLM (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings, supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: G-quadruplex structures act as replication road blocks and these regions are recombinational hot spots.
source: G-quadruplex structures were shown to act as replication road blocks and these regions were shown to be recombinational hot spots (van Wietmarschen et al., 2018; Rhodes and Lipps, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to van Wietmarschen et al., 2018; Rhodes and Lipps, 2015.

claim: RecQ helicases can efficiently unwind G-quadruplex structures.
source: RecQ helicases can efficiently unwind G-quadruplex structures, possibly to aid DNA replication, suppress genome instability and to influence transcription of various genes (Voter et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Voter et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2016.

claim: The HRDC domain of human BLM helicase is essential for efficient, repetitive unwinding of G-quadruplexes.
source: In line with this idea, the HRDC domain of human BLM helicase was shown to be essential for efficient, repetitive unwinding of G-quadruplexes Chatterjee et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chatterjee et al., 2014.

claim: SSB is displaced by RecQ despite the much higher apparent binding affinity of SSB for ssDNA.
source: For example, single-strand binding protein (SSB) would likely compete with the HRDC for ssDNA binding. However, we recently demonstrated that SSB is displaced by RecQ despite the much higher apparent binding affinity of SSB for ssDNA (Mills et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mills et al., 2017.
